title: Birth of Shree Krishna
body:
Birth of Shree Krishna

For days Parikshith had listened, spellbound, as Shuka Maharishi unfolded the many descents of Sriman Narayana. But there was one avatara his heart longed above all to hear of — the one in which the Supreme did not appear briefly for a single purpose, but chose to walk among men, to grow as a child, to play, to teach, and to restore the world to its divine rhythm. He asked the sage to narrate the story of Krishna, whose very name grants liberation, and Shuka, his own soul immersed in the glories of Govinda, closed his eyes in bliss and began.
The weight of adharma upon the earth had grown unbearable. Kings had forsaken righteousness, tyrants waged wars that shook the balance of the world, and Bhoomi Devi could no longer endure the burden pressing upon her. Taking the form of a sorrowful cow, she ascended to Brahma and wept, telling him that she could bear mountains and oceans and storms, but not the wickedness that had spread across the land, of which Kansa, the tyrant king of Mathura, was the greatest. Brahma knew this was a matter for the Supreme alone, and he gathered the Devas and led them to Vaikuntham, where Sriman Narayana rested upon Adishesha. There Bhoomi Devi fell at the Lord's feet and pleaded with Him to descend and restore balance before dharma was lost forever.
The Lord, ever merciful, assured her that He would descend and establish dharma once more. He drew forth two locks of His hair, one black and one white, signifying that this time He would descend not as one but as two — Krishna and Balarama. He would be born, He declared, as the son of Devaki and Vasudeva, and His elder brother to Rohini, and together they would rid the world of its burdens.
Devaki was the daughter of Ugrasena, king of Mathura. On the day of her marriage to Vasudeva, once the ceremonies were complete, it was customary for the couple to ride together through the city, and Devaki's brother Kansa, in a show of affection, took it upon himself to drive their chariot. No sooner had the couple mounted than a voice sounded from the sky, foretelling that the eighth child born of Devaki and Vasudeva would be the cause of Kansa's destruction. His joy twisting into terror, Kansa seized his sister by the hair and drew his sword to kill her on the spot. But Vasudeva stayed his hand, asking why he should fear one yet unborn, and vowing to deliver every child of theirs into his hands. Kansa relented, but imprisoned the couple to ensure the promise was kept.
One by one the children were born, and one by one six of them perished at their uncle's hands. The seventh child was spared by divine intervention, transferred to the womb of Rohini in Gokul and declared to the world a miscarriage; that child was Balarama. When Devaki carried her eighth child, every sign ran contrary to nature. Where an expecting mother usually grows pale, Devaki grew dark and radiant; when she walked she felt as though she were gliding, for Garuda was said to attend her; when she slept the floor seemed to shift beneath her, for Adishesha himself served as her bed. On the eighth night of the dark fortnight of Shraavan, amid roaring thunder and the swelling of the Yamuna, the Supreme chose to descend. A golden radiance filled the prison cell, and Sriman Narayana appeared before Devaki and Vasudeva in His divine form. At their trembling wonder He assured them their suffering was at an end, and, at Devaki's request, took on the form of an ordinary human infant, instructing that He be carried to Gokul. As He did so, the prison doors unlocked and the guards fell into deep slumber.
